At a Meeting of the SuRTEES Society, held in 
Durham Castle on March 5th, tg01, the DEAN OF 
DuRHAM in the chair, 


It was resolved, 


That the first Volume of the year 1900 be Vol. III 
of the Account Rolls of the Abbey of Durham, edited 
by CANON FOWLER. 

WILLIAM BROWN, 


Secretary. 


Tabi Eee ks ne COT 


———____ —___ 


Tuts third and concluding volume has been delayed 
longer than was expected by the preparation of the Intro- 
duction, the Glossary, the Lists of Subjects, and the Index. 
.The notes promised in the Preface to Vol. II have been 
taken into the Glossary, in the final revision of which 
I have received valuable help from Mr. F. Adams, whose 
services in connexion with the Metrical Life of St. 
Cuthbert are mentioned. in the Preface to the Surtees 
Society's edition of that work, and from Mr. R. Oliver 
Heslop, the learned and obliging editor of the Northumber- 
land Glossary, as well as from the friends named in 
the Introduction to the present volume, pp. Ixvi, Ixvii. 


Briefly to review the contents of this volume, I may 
say that the concluding portion of the Bursars’ Rolls 
will, I think, be found not less valuable than the earlier 
portion. Many points of interest in these rolls are referred 
to in the Introduction, pp. xxiii—xxx. The Rotuli de 
Miners illustrate the position of the Prior and Convent as 
coal-owners and coal-workers. The Jscellanea are 
extracts from the papers referred to in the Preface to Vol. 
I, as having led to the compilation of this whole collection, 
and, together with the extracts from Treasurers’ Books, 
almost wholly relate to the periods next after the Dissolu- 
Momeeor the monastery. At p. 718, however, is an 
interesting little Prior’s roll of 1356-7. 


The Index is, at any rate, a very full one, and I have 
tried to make it as good as I could in every respect. To 
construct a faultless Index, itself occupying 122 pages, 
would be, I think, beyond the power of most people. 
I regret that this one was not reserved till after the 
completion of the Glossary ; had this been done, the list 
of amendments, p. 867, would have been much shorter 
than it is. The lists of Subjects, pp. 870-886, are 


\2 5309 


Vill PREFACE. 


intended to be used with the Index, and to supply the 
place of a classified index, so that, after all, I trust that the 
apparatus for purposes of reference will be found to be 
fairly complete. Since the list on p. 887 was printed, 
explanations of four of the words have been found, and are 
provided in the Glossary and Corrigenda. Others will be 
gladly received at any time. I have taken great pains with 
the Glossary. If some inequality of treatment be observed, 
it is to be borne in mind that some of the words are very 
curious and uncommon, and that the notes originally 
intended have been, as is mentioned above, included in the 
Glossary, which also contains the less familiar names of 
persons and places occurring in the Rolls. Names of 
places that I have not been able to identify are, like 
unexplained words, left with references to pages only. 


With regard to the Introduction, I need only refer to 
what is said on p. Ixiii of the same. 


And now that the Rolls are off my hands, I hope at 
once to complete the preparation of Az¢es of Durham, that 
it may be issued in a few months’ time. 


DURHAM, 
OCTOBER, 1901.

with the annual and other payments to the Dean, the 
twelve prebendaries, twelve minor canons, readers of 
Gospel and Epistle (not necessarily minor canons), ten 
lay clerks, master of choristers, ten choristers, eight 
poor men, subdean, treasurer, sacrist, precentor, two 
vergers, two bellringers, head master of school, second 
master, eighteen scholars, three annuitants, receiver, 
outer porter, inner porter, two bakers, two cooks, forester 
of Bearpark, park-keeper of same, bailiff of Shields, keeper 
of Baxter wood, bailiff of Elvet, keeper of Haning wood, 
registrar, clerk of the works, bailiffs of Framwellgate and 
of Billingham, three travelling bailiffs, bailiff of Shores- 
wood, repairer of glass windows, vicars of St. Oswald’s, 
Durham, Norham, and Bywell Peter, curate of St- 
Margaret’s, Durham, vicar of Berwick, chaplain of St. 
Mary’s chantry in church of St. Nicholas, Durham, rector 
of South Bailey, chaplain of Hilton in Wakerfield, rector of 
Muggleswick, chaplains of Heworth, of Ferry, of chantry 
of St. James in church of St. Nicholas, of St. Mary in St. 
Margaret’s, of St. Mary in St. Nicholas’, of the Holy 
Trinity in the same, of St. Mary Magdalene, of St. Mary 
in St. Oswald’s, the guild of St. Cuthbert, remesgae 
for aqueduct, in Gilesgate, a tenement, landmale to the 
bishop for waste at Framwellgate, the Queen for proceeds 
of above chantries.

having as a watermark a glove and star. The roll is 
imperfect at the top, and has never contained any 
account of expenses. The rents of each place are 
entered ina lump sum. The places are the same as 
in the Bursars’ rolls, but differently arranged. The 
first series ends thus :—

May it please yow to vnderstand right worshipfull that 
whereas yow have one pare of Orgaynes w% standeth above 
the Quere doore, & haith not bene played vpon thes many 
yeres for lacke of mendinge, I have bestowed a weekes 
labor in mendinge the sownd boord, the wynd stopp, the 
Springe wyers, and in tuninge the pipes, so that I have 
mayd them in that good order as now they will much 
delight bothe the auditorie and the player because they 
yeld the most principallest and imperiali sound of all the 
rest. And if it seame strainge vnto yor worshipes that I 
have tayken in hand to doe it, yow shall vnderstand that I 
have had some practise in mendinge of an Instrument, 
and also I have geven diligence in markinge men of 
greater skill that haith bene here in tymes passed when 
they have been recompensed five markes or fortie shillinges 
for lesse paynes than I have taken (wc) I referr to the 
quere) so that now I leve my paynes to yor good considera- 
tions, for because I did not so much seeke after the 
recompence of rewarde as I did the excellencie of the 
Instrumente regarde, and as also that yow should see my 
redinesse & good will to indevour my selfe in what soev' 
I may to profitt ot Churche.

The following notes of expenses ought to have come 
in next after p. 719, but were overlooked in consequence of 
their being kept separately from the rest, framed and 
glazed in the Chapter Library. The frames are made of 
oak from the original boards of Bishop Pudsey’s Bible. 
Dr. Raine has given extracts from the accounts in “St. 
Cuthbert,” 1787., 179. He says that they were both 
“extracted from a bundle of bills in the Treasury for 1542, 
under which year are comprised the expences of the 
Church from Michaelmas, 1541, to the same day in the 
following year.” The short note of a payment of 15d. 
to ‘* Rayffe Skelus” (also printed by Raine in his note 
on p. 178 above referred to) was found by me among the 
miscellaneous charters.

AQUEDUCTUS, a leaden water-pipe often called a conduit, by which water 
was brought to the Abbey, to Beaurepaire, or elsewhere; the 
medieval lead pipes, like those of the Romans, were made with a seam 
along the side, the lengths being joined by collars ; the seams and 
joints were usually ‘‘ burned,” not soldered. A Cundyth, aguaductile : 
C, A. and note. It is said in a MS. of about the time of James _I, 
quoted in the Introduction to ‘‘ Study of the Pipe Rolls,’ that it 
was supposed that ‘‘our Ancestors... tooke their plott from an 
aqueduct. That as water is derived from many springes to heades, 
and from heades guided into a pipe, and by that carried into the 
cesterne of a greate house or pallace, where it is to bee expended 
accordinge to the necessitie and use of every office. Soe, this silver 
streame, growing out of divers natures, might bee drawne from its 
springes, wch are the severale courtes from whence it ariseth, to 
certaine heades, from thence collected into one pipe, and by that 
conveyed into the cesterne, wch is his Mates receipte.” For the 
details of water distribution at Canterbury as shown in Norman 
drawings, see Willis, Conventual Buildings, ch. x.

GELOFFERS, cloves; see Clowys. The original name of the spice was 
girofie or gilofre, from late Lat. carophilum, from Greek Kapuogudror ;

latter name has passed to other scented flowers, and has been 
further perverted to July-fower. In the Rolls the spice is sometimes 
called Clowes and sometimes Geloffers. See N. E. D. on Clove, 
Clove-gillyflower, and Gillyflower.

GLOSSARY. 1923 


HAyRES, haircloths. (1) For drying the malt in kilns after it has begun to put 
out rootlets, but before it sprouts. In Harrison’s Desc. of England, 
1586, bk. II, ch. vi, is a full account of the process, where it is said 
that ‘‘ they carie it to a kill covered with a haire cloth.” This use of 
haircloth was common in the eighteenth century, and is perhaps not 
yet wholly obsolete. ‘‘ There are several methods used in drying of 
Malts, as the Iron Plate Frame, the Tile Frame, that are both full of 
little holes ; the Brass-wired and Iron-wired Frame, and the Hair- 
cloth; . . . by many the Hair-cloth is reckoned the best of all”’ ; 
The London and Country Brewer, London, 1759, quoted in Stopes, 
Malt and Malting, London, 1885, p. 25. Stopes speaks of hair cloth 
as stiff horse hair woven into a coarse mesh, but ‘‘ seldom used.” The 
hair cloth and woven wire were stretched on frames, or, when used on 
larger scale, fastened to the walls of the heated chambers and 
supported by wooden bars resting on joists. The heat employed is 
not so great as to injure the hair. Haircloth has also been much 
used in drying saffron. (2) To wear for mortification of the flesh ; 
C. A. 170, xliv. (3) For under-coverings of altars, as also at Norwich, 
‘‘hayre pro altaribus,” Rot. Sacr., 1400-1. (4) For hair-sieves.

RATONES, ‘rattons,” rats. Ratun, or raton; Rato, sorex: P. P., so 
©. A, z.e., the old English black rat (Mus Rattus), which has rapidly 
disappeared before the now common brown or Norway rat (Mus 
decumanus), but it survived about Durham Cathedral until about 
1882, when the last was trapped. Canon Greenwell remembers a 
good many being in and about the church. 

RATONROWE, now represented by Court Lane, which connects Old and 
New Elvet; the name appears to have been changed when the 
Assize Courts were removed to the top of Elvet. There are, or 
have been, almost as many Raton Rawes as High Streets and Kirk- 
gates in Northern towns, and the origin of the name has been much 
discussed in Motes and Queries as well as elsewhere. Out of some 
eight or ten derivations that have been suggested, the most likely 
seems to be that it was a depreciatory designation applied 
to rows of mean houses infested with ratons or rats, hence, prover- 
bially, a poor row of houses. The term Vicus Rattonum occurs A.D. 
1458 in a Glasgow Cartulary, and Raton Rawe seems to have been 
the most usual form before it took the modern form of ‘ Rotten 
Row.”

REGRATOR, one who buys goods in a market in order to sell them at a 
higher price in the same market. To do this was a punishable 
offence. See Nottingham Records, V, 292, 343. But any retail 
dealer was called a Regrator or Regrateress, as distinct from the 
Engrosser (grocer) or wholesale dealer. Regratresses received 
from the bakers thirteen loaves to the dozen at the price of twelve, 
their profit lying in the.thirteenth loaf. Hence the ‘‘ baker’s dozen.” 
Skeat, Notes to P. Plowman, p. 43.

SCUTUM DE BRAUNE, 24, 32, Clifeus apri, 53. De braun j scutum et 
dimidium : Jarrow Rolls, p. 34. The term ‘‘ shield of brawn” is not 
unknown in English literature. In the 1867 edition of Nares’s 
Glossary are these quotations: ‘‘ No weapons in the age to come be 
known But shield of bacon, and the sword of brawn,” Randolph’s 
Jealous Lovers, 1646; ‘‘ like a shield of brawn at Shrovetide, out of 
date’’: Poor Robin, 1705. And in ‘‘Ivanhoe” we are told that 
Wamba, the jester, ‘‘ opposed to the beard of the Jew a shield of 
brawn, which he plucked from beneath his cloak.” Nares does not 
give any explanation of the term, which does not occur in any of the 
many dictionaries and glossaries besides Nares’s that I have 
consulted. Halliwell gives ‘‘Shield-bones, Blade-bones, /orth.,” 
quoting from the Legend of Sir Guy, ‘‘ One of his sheeld-bones to 
this day Hangs in the citye of Coventrye.” This might suggest that 
a ‘**Shield of brawn” was the shoulder of a boar. But it appears 
that the skin of the boar, whether raw or tanned, is called a boar’s 
shield >}-N. and Q., 7th S., X, 353, cf 2nd S., X, 478, at which 
second reference we find that ‘‘in brawn-making this shield is placed 
round the inside of a cylindrical mould, and the middle filled up with 
the meat and fat properly prepared. It is then subjected to many 
hours boiling,”” which gelatinizes the tough hide, and makes it 


61 


962 GLOSSARY. 


eatable. Our modern brawn would seem to be ‘‘a shield of brawn ° 
with the shield left out, and it is made of any pig, not, as it should 
be, of boar only. In a description of the ‘‘unlacing” of a boar in 
‘Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight” (E.E.T.S.), c. A.D. 1360, 1. 1611, 
occurs this line, ““Sypen he britnez out pe brawen in bryst brode 
[s]cheldes”’ (Then he cuts out the brawn in bright broad shields), and 
in the same poem, 1. 1456, in connexion with a boar hunt, is this 
passage, ‘‘Bot pe poynte3 payred at pe pyth pat py3t in his schelde3”’ 
(the arrow-points failed in power that stuck in his shields). Guillim 
says, after mentioning that the boar has “his Target to defend 
himself,’ that ‘‘the Shield of a Boare well managed, is a good 
Buckler against that cruell Enemy called Hunger”: Display of 
Heraldry, 1660, p. 176. It would seem, then, that a shield of brawn 
was (1) The hide of the boar, (2) a shield or buckler made thereof, 
(3) boar’s flesh enveloped therein.

SEPULCHRE, 715, 728. The ‘‘Easter Sepulchre,” usually a wooden 
receptacle more or less ornamented, in which the Blessed Sacrament 
and the Crucifix were deposited from Good Friday to Easter morn- 
ing. It was commonly set up in a recess on the north side of the 
chancel, and was, while in use, decorated with drapery attached by 
tacks and pins, and had candles burning before it. See Bloxham, 
Goth. Archit., 1882, Vol. II, 93—124; Chambers, Divine Worship, 
1877, xxx—xl; Processionale Sarum, Leeds, 1882, pp. 72, 91; 
Proc. Ebor. in ‘‘ York Manual, etc.,” Surtees Soc., pp. 163, 170; 
Ludlow Ch. W.. Accts., Camd. Soc., 3, 7, 11, etc. ; Rolls, 418. We 
find 1d. spent ‘‘ in tackettes to sett vp ye sepulchre”’ for Easter, 1548 
(2 Edw. VI), and a new sepulchre made of wainscot, Mar. 26, 1558, 
a fortnight before Easter Even (4 and 5 Phil. and Mary). The 
earlier one had probably been destroyed.

estuaries until they were poisoned by chemical works, mines, and 


sewage. Where ‘‘sprots”’ are mentioned in the Rolls, it is probable 
that smelts are meant. See Sperlinges.

TALLIA, tally, a stick split in two parts, on each of which is notched a 
debtor’s and creditor's account, one part being kept by each person. 
As no other two pieces would fit each to each, there can be no 
cheating by means of a false tally. Bundles of tally sticks may 
probably still be seen hanging on bakers’ carts in France and else- 
where, each bearing some mark to identify it with the customer who 
is retaining the corresponding piece. So here we find the Cellarer 
and the Bursar keeping accounts by tally, p. 1. On Exchequer 
tallies, see Intr. to Study of Pipe Rolls, 64, 96 (plate p. 66). See 
also Round, Calendar of Documents preserved in France, I, 465.

ULNAGIUM, ULNACIO, 527, ulnage or alnage, the measuring of cloth by the 
ell, testing its quality and collecting alnage duty for the Crown. In

Hartlepool to take ‘‘ prisz,” 7z.e., certain proportions of wine

likewise ‘‘ officium ulnariz pannorum de partibus transmarinis” : 
Kellaw’s Reg., Rolls ed. IV, 295. And it is possible that there may 
be some confusion between gauging and ulnage in the one passage 
in these extracts where the latter business is referred to. The term 
‘“‘Ullage”’ is, however, now applied to the decrease which takes 
place in the quantity of wine in a bottle.

THE period covered by these volumes begins with the 
year 1091, in which the Benedictine monks were first 
established in Durham, and ends with 1540, the year of the 
dissolution of the monastery. The only officers of whom 
we find mention in connexion with the coming of the 
monks are the Bishop, the Prior, and the Sacrist,2 though 
there may have been others. The Bishop, as in other 
monastic cathedral churches, took the place of the Abbot, 
and he still occupies not only the episcopal throne in the 
choir and seat in the chapter-house, but the right-hand 
stall on entering the choir, which the Abbot would have in 
an ordinary abbey. The Benedictine Rule names the 
Abbot, Prior, Cellarer, Porter, and also certain officers 
called Decani, each of whom originally may have had the 
charge of ten other monks. Their office, however, seems 
to have fallen into abeyance at a comparatively early period, 
and it is not recognized in the Cistercian system.3 Nor do we 
find any reference to it inthe Durham Rolls, although there 
were two “‘decani ordinis” in 1437 and in 1501.4 Their 
position was probably maintained more in theoretical 
compliance with the Rule than for any practical purpose. 


In Durham, however, there was special need for a 
Sacrist, an officer not mentioned in the Benedictine Rule. 
For the church of Durham possessed the sacred body of 

St. Cuthbert, with all that belonged to it, and required 
some one person specially responsible for the charge of 
such priceless treasures. In later times this part of the 
Sacrist’s duty, originally the main part, devolved on a 
separate officer called the Feretrar or Shrine-Keeper, who 
had a colleague, as well as a subordinate or two.

11 INTRODUCTION. 


It is not known when the system of Obedientiaries or 
monastic officers, each having his own special duties, 
received its full development.t The earliest account roll we 
have is dated 1278: its contents are similar to those of a 
Bursar’s roll, but it is not so called in the heading.2 The 
first mention of a Bursar is in 1293.3 In the former half of 
the fourteenth century, we find at Durham a Hostillar, 
Cellarer, Almoner, Sacrist, Chamberlain, and Master of the 
Infirmary,4 who were all monks, appointed to their 
several offices by the Prior, after more or less of consulta- 
tion with the members of his monastic chapter. In 1375 
we find a Feretrar, in 1401 a Terrar or land-agent, and in 
1416 a Commoner or keeper of the common-house. The 
dates to which I have referred are only those of the earliest 
of the rolls that happen to have survived. But we may 
say that the system of Obedientiaries or special officers had 
long been fully developed in Durham, as elsewhere, in the 
fourteenth century, and was always subject to still further 
divisions of labour as time went on and duties became more 
complicated and onerous. 


The number of monks in Durham, was, as elsewhere, 
variable. In 1409 there were 27, including the Prior, at one 
time, and 31 at another.5 About the same time there were 
32.6 In 1437, 61.7 In 1446 there were 49 in Durham and 
30 in the cells; in 1456, 71 in Durham and cells; in 1501, 
43 in Durham. With these numbers we may compare 64 
at Winchester in 1325,9 35 at Selby about 1436,' and 25 in 
1465.7° In point of numbers, the English Benedictine 
houses rarely attained to the ideal number, which was 70,

We have seen that in Durham, as in Winchester, Ely, 
and other monastic Cathedrals, the Bishop was the honorary 
and titular head, while the true head of the house was the 
Prior, But the Bishop concerned himself little with 
monastic affairs. A part of Bishop William’s scheme 
for the establishing of the Benedictine monks had been 
to effect a separation of the estates into those of the 
monastery and those of the Bishop. The Lord Prior 
was the working head of the Abbey, and he came 
to rank with Abbots. Prior Robert Berrington, of 
Walworth, who succeeded in 1374, obtained the use of the 
mitre and crosier, and so became, as a mitred Abbot, a 
personage of much more distinction than one who was not 
mitred. In 1431 the Abbot of St. Alban’s, the Prior 
of Durham and the Abbot of Pershore were the three 
Presidents of the Benedictine Order in England. In 1465 
the Prior of Durham held a visitation of all the Benedictine 
Abbeys in the Province of York.« But the: Lord Prior, 
besides being so eminent an ecclesiastic, was a great 
county magnate, ranking with the Nevilles of Raby and 
Brancepeth, the Percys of Alnwick, and the rest of the 
northern nobles, while in Durham itself he kept a state 
Only a little inferior to that of the great Prince Bishop 
himself. He had his residence apart from the monks, as 
- was usual, but the mansion of the Priors of Durham, now 
the Deanery, was, as indeed it still is, quite fit to be a 
Bishop’s Palace. Only on great and rare occasions did the 
Prior appear in the Refectory. He lived in such state as 
was then thought befitting, with his own chaplain, clerks, 
esquires, seneschal, and servants. All wore his splendid 
liveries, according to their rank, just as in other great 
houses. We find numberless entries in the Rolls relating 
to the various coloured cloths for these liveries, and to the 
costly furs and other materials required for the robes of the 


* Selby Cartulary, I, 347.

Prior himself. He travelled about the county and 
sojourned at his manors of Bearpark, Pittington, Wardley, 
Bewley, Dalton, and so on, with a great retinue, 
distributing alms as he passed along the roads on his 
handsomely appointed palfrey. Thus he was held in great 
reverence not only for his ecclesiastical dignity but for his 
position as a temporal magnate. He kept a great number 
of palfreys and other horses, as well as hounds and falcons. 
And we find frequent mention of the /onga carecta or long 
cart, the horses of which were harnessed in red leather. 
This was used to carry the ‘‘chapel’’! and other belongings 
of the Prior and his household from place to place, and, 
when all the articles were safely packed, they were 
protected from rain and dust by hides sewn together and 
secured by cords, thus serving the same purpose as 
tarpaulins do at the present time. I regret to say that on 
one occasion the Bursar had to be warned to ‘‘ elongate’? 
the wood cart, lest it should be taken away by the king’s 
servants.3 There is only one roll remaining of the account 
of the Lord Prior’s Master of the Horse, of the date 1420.4 
It appears that there was a great stud farm at Beaurepaire, 
now Bearpark, where horses were bred and trained. Such 
of these as were not required for use were sold at fairs, as 
at Ripon, Darlington, and Durham. At Durham Fair the 
folds for the horses were set up in Gilesgate. Some horses 
were bought from time to time, at various prices. There 
was enough pasture at Beaurepaire to enable the Abbey to 
gain a little profit by taking in horses to grass, at the rate 
of 3s. 4d. a head from the Invention of the Holy Cross 
(May 3) to Michaelmas Day (Sept. 29). The Bishop 
Suffragan once owed 3s. 4d. for his horse, but was excused 
payment. This great stud farm at Beaurepaire, in charge of 
an officer who appears to have been one of the Prior’s 
household, helps us to realize how important a personage 
the Prior was.

vi INTRODUCTION. 


The enjoyment of social pleasures, however, and the 
delights of country life, formed by no means the only 
occupation of the Prior. His was a place of great 
responsibility as chief administrator of the convent. He 
presided, when at home, at the daily and weekly Chapter. 
He-was, next after the Bishop, the chief figure and host in 
hospitality shown to kings, queens, nobles, prelates, and 
other distinguished ecclesiastics and layfolk. There were 
great banquets on the feasts of St. Cuthbert in March and 
September, as well as at Christmas, Easter, and other high 
festivals. Sometimes the Prior gave banquets on a grand 
scale to the Bishop of Durham and to the great people 
invited to meet the princely prelate. Indeed, as we read in 
the Rites of Durham, he ‘‘did keppe a moste honorable 
house and very noble intertaynement, being attended upon 
both with gentlemen and yeomen, of the best in the 
countrie, as the honorable service of his house deserved no 
lesse.” Then, of course, in all the great functions that 
took place in the Cathedral Church, the Prior took the 
place next after the Bishop. His importance as a feudal 
lord is illustrated by some very curious rolls headed 
Marescalcia Prioris, which show how his officers went to 
the various towns and villages within his jurisdiction, and 
held courts of assize for the purpose of testing weights and 
measures, and the quality of bread and ale offered for sale, 
and for punishing by fine or by burning of measures those 
whose measures were found to be wrong either way, or 
whose bread and ale or other things sold were below the 
mark in quality or in quantity. We should hardly expect 
people to be fined for having their weights and measures 
above the standard, but fines are inflicted for the same kind 
of inaccuracy at the present time, e.g., a person was fined 
for having a 4 lb. weight-11% drachms in excess of the 
standard in January, i1go1.t And to put a check 
upon such slovenly trading was only in accordance 
with that beneficent rule which the Priors exercised 
wheresoever their jurisdiction prevailed... If the Priors 
were great county magnates and dignified ecclesiastics, 
it by no means follows that they were in the habit

of either neglecting their responsibilities or of abusing 
their great powers. And perhaps I cannot better conclude 
this notice of them than in the words of one of their 
successors, the present Dean of Durham, who, in the 
Introduction to his valuable work on the Winchester 
Account Rolls, writes words no less applicable in the 
northern than in the southern city. ‘‘We prefer to see,” 
he says, ‘‘in the Prior, a great noble, ruling over what was 
far better than a noble’s fortress—a well-ordered, peaceful 
community, which on the one side kept up a perpetual 
protest against the rude vices of the age, and on the other 
side showed to the kings, nobles, and prelates who 
thronged our city, the pattern of an organization for the 
conduct of life and business which could hardly have been 
found elsewhere in medizval times.” 


THE SUB-PRIOR. 


Next after the Lord Prior came the Sub-Prior, usually, 
we may suppose, an elderly monk who had deserved well 
of the convent, and had, perhaps, come in second at the 
last election of a Prior. In Durham he was Master of the 
Frater or Refectory, and he slept in the dormitory of the 
monks in a chamber over the door, so constructed that he 
might hear if any one went out. We learn from the A7¢es 
of Durham that he exercised the office of Circa or 
watchman, going round to every monk’s chamber to see 
that he was in his place. He presided at the monks’ table 
in the misericorde or Loft, said grace at their dinner and 
supper, saw that the doors about the monastery were locked 
and unlocked at the appointed times, kept the keys at 
night, and delivered them in the morning to those who had 
charge of them during the day. Like the Prior, he 
sometimes went out to sojourn at the manors, taking with 
him some other monks, that they might enjoy a little 
holiday together. During the absences of the Prior from 
Durham, the Sub-Prior took his place. At all times his 
duty was to exercise a general supervision of the monastic 
household, as distinct from that of the Prior, which was 
managed by the Prior’s Chaplain.2 As the Prior. of

Durham was practically an Abbot, so the Sub-Prior’s 
duties were to some extent those of the Prior in most 
abbeys. 


THE THIRD PRIOR. 


There was also in Durham, as elsewhere, a ‘‘ third 
Prior,” as he was sometimes called, who acted in place of 
the Sub-Prior if necessary. In Durham he was called the 
Deece Prior, but why so called I cannot say. - We could 
have understood the Sub-Prior’s being called the Deece (or 
Dais) Prior, for he presided at the meals of the monks in 
the Loft, and said grace, as we have just now seen. But 
the Deece Prior is described in Aztes as a different man. 
At the time of the Dissolution this office was held by the 
Master of the Feretory.: At Winchester there was 
sometimes a ‘‘ fourth Prior.’’? 


THE PRIOR’S CHAPLAIN. 


The Priors Chaplain was a very important person, 
having the whole charge of the Prior’s great household, as 
well as of the services conducted in the Prior’s private 
chapel. His office, or place of business, called ‘*The 
Chaplain’s Checker,” was over the stairs leading to the 
Prior’s hall, now the Dean’s ante-room and dining-room. 
He received from the Bursar the sums required for the 
Prior’s housekeeping and apparel, had charge of the plate 
and other treasure, and paid the gentlemen, yeomen, and 
other officers and servants of the household. His sleeping 
chamber was next to that of the Prior.3 He constantly 
appears in the Bursar’s Rolls as ordering the Garderoba 
or household requisites for the Prior, and is often called 
simply ‘‘ Capellanus.”’ 


Besides the Chaplain, the Prior’s household included 
a Chamberlain,4 Esquires, Valecti both lay and clerical, 
other clerks, a Supervisor Equicii ?,5 Palfrey man, grooms, 
pages, cook, messengers, errand-boys, and the like, much 
as in any other great establishment.

INTRODUCTION. 1X 


Thus supported and attended on, the Lord Prior 
presided over all the various departments of the convent, 
each of which had its own chief officer. These departments 
may be divided into three classes, namely :— 

1. Those connected with the conduct of Divine 
Service, the sustentation of the fabric, and the care of the 
shrines, the furniture, and the ornaments of the church and 
of the ministers thereof. The two chief officers in this class 
were the Sacrist and the Feretrar, with whom may be 
reckoned their colleagues, assistants, or deputies, among 
whom the Sub-Sacrist frequently occurs, and the Vicars, a 
class of officers not to be found in the accounts of other 
monastic churches, so far as I know. Then there were 
minor officers, such as thuriblers, bell-ringers, banner- 
bearers, the five clericuli or pueri ecclesie, one puer or 
-gromus ecclesic,' and, in short, all who were employed in 
the church in any way. The ‘‘congregation” at the 
ordinary services consisted of the monks and_ novices, 
though others may have been admitted occasionally. 

2. The second class included the monastic household 
as distinct from the Prior’s establishment, which was, as 
we have seen, superintended by his Chaplain. The 
Obedientiaries or monastic officers of the Abbey were 
_the Bursar, the Terrar, the Hostillar, the Cellarer, the 
Chamberlain, the Master of the Common-house, the Master 
of the Garners, the Master of the Infirmary, the Almoner, 
the Master fe the Novices, the Master of the Song 
School, or Cantor, and the Schoolmaster of the 
Ghiltiren of the Almery.2 The daily occupations of most 
of these officers are illustrated by the Rolls, as will be 
briefly indicated in the present Introduction, and 
abundantly shown by a perusal of the original matter that 
forms the main part of these volumes. 

3. The third class was concerned with the estates 
of the Abbey, the care of which threw upon the Prior no 
light burden of practical business, for he was the true

the recreations of a country gentleman. Here in Durham 
he was aided by his Seneschal, and by the Terrar, the 
Bursar, and the Master of the Garners, as well as by other 
officers, who had their own separate estates to manage, 
namely, the Sacrist, the Almoner, and the Hostillar, and

Thus these three departments may be briefly

THE SACRTSA: 

In Artes he is called ‘‘ Maister Segerstan,” which 
was doubtless his usual designation. His checker or 
office was in the angle formed by the north transept 
and the north aisle of the choir, on the walls of which 
distinct traces of it may still be seen. It had a door 
from the north aisle, the opening for which is now blocked 
up. The Sacrist provided altar-bread and wine, wax, 
lights, and incense. He kept always a tun of wine in his 
checker for use in the Church. He saw that the glass 
windows were kept in repair, and plumber’s work attended 
to when required ; he was also responsible for the keeping 
in order of the bells, and the cleaning of the Church. He 
kept the keys of the various aumbries, and laid them out 
every morning between six and seven o’clock, that the 
monks might take them when they went to say mass. He 
was responsible for the plate and other valuables kept in 
the aumbries. He managed the estate of Sacristonheugh. 
His bedchamber was in the dormitory, and his meat was 
served from the great kitchen to his checker,! so that he 
appears, as do some of the other officers, not to have taken 
his meals, as a rule, with the other monks. We have a 
good number of the account rolls and inventories of the 
Sacrists. The earliest that is left is of the year 1318.

INTRODUCTION. XI 


Copious extracts from them are printed in our second 
volume.' These are full of references to the kind of things 
mentioned in Az¢es, but, of course, they go into much 
more detail. For instance, as at Norwich, and doubtless 
in all great churches, there was a place mtecidéd over by 
the magister cere and called the Wax-house, where the 
wax and candle-wick were kept, and the candles and 
torches made. The wax was melted over a charcoal fire 
and worked on a large metal plate. The Sacrist had a 
brass mould for making some candles. A great quantity 
of wax was burnt in every church in the course of a year, 
and to supply the demand it seems likely that more bees 
were kept than at present; these would also supply the 
honey, of which so much more was consumed before the 
universal use of sugar came in. The great torches that 
“were carried in processions were made of wax and resin 
mixed, as was the case at Ripon,3 and no doubt generally. 
For purposes of light there were the cressets, earthen 
basins, or else great facle of stone with cup-like cavities 
in which was burnt fat from the kitchen, with a floating 
wick in each cavity. Such cresset-stones have been found 
and are to be seen in various places,+ but none of the 
Durham ones are known to be in existence. For sym- 
bolical purposes, as in the case of altar-lights or lights 
near the altar, or before sacred pictures or images, or 
around the bodies of the faithful departed, nothing was 
used but pure wax, which was felt to be more appropriate 
than anything else, not only by reason of its pure bright 
light, but as being made by the innocent industrious bees 
from God’s own flowers, and as having no such unlovely 
associations about it as tallow and things of that sort have. 
Indeed there is no artificial light to compare in beauty with 
that of wax candles, and therefore none so fit for the sacred 
purposes to which it is applied. Nevertheless, in Durham, 
as in all great churches, there were, hanging before the

These were partly symbolical no doubt, but, in any case,

He also provided the altar-bread and wine for the 
celebration of the masses that were sung in the church 
day by day at some thirty altars. The bread was always 
in the form of wafers made of the finest flour that could 
be obtained from picked grains of the best wheat. These 
wafers were commonly called ‘‘ obleys,’” which word is 
a short form of the word ‘‘oblation,” and they were 
made by pinching the paste between a pair of nippers 
called ‘‘obley-irons,” or ‘‘baking-irons,”’ previously heated. 
at a fire of charcoal. There was a fireplace in which 
this was done, in the thickness of the wall in the south 
transept, but it has been blocked up and the outside 
chimney destroyed in some of the earlier ‘‘ restorations ” 
to which the church has been subjected. The opening 
through which the chimney went up still exists, with 
a moulding carried round it, in the wooden ceiling of 
the cloisters. This same fireplace may have served to 
supply the glowing embers for the thuribles. The obleys 
were sometimes bought at York, by the hundred. There 
is no mention of any special kind of wine. The Sacrist 
would see that the holy-water basins were properly 
supplied, and for making the holy water a small quantity of 
salt was required: accordingly there was a silver scallop 
for blessing salt. Another thing that had to be provided 
was incense, and this is frequently mentioned in the 
Rolls. One great part of the Sacrist’s duty was to look 
after the vestments, and to see that they were repaired 
or renewed as they became partly worn, or worn out.

material, tough as it is. Sometimes a bell would 
become cracked and require to be recast. This was 
usually done on the spot, as was bell-casting generally 
at that time, it being formerly more convenient for the 
bell-founder to carry his materials and other requisites 
from place to place, than to convey the bells either to 
or from the foundry. Nevertheless we have a curious 
story about Prior Turgot having a heavy bell cast in 
London at the end of the eleventh century and brought — 
to Durham on a truck drawn by twenty-two oxen,' but 
this was exceptional. The Sacrist’s Roll of 1413-14 
contains an interesting account of the casting and hang- 
ing of six new bells, with the making of everything 
belonging to them, followed by a subscription list.2 
The old metal was used, with new added, and no doubt 
the metal of Prior Turgot’s bell and of others in Eald- 
hune’s church is included in the present bells, all of 
which have been recast in modern times. When the 
Neville screen was sent down from London, ‘as is men- 
tioned more particularly at the end of the section on the 
Bursars’ Rolls, the Sacrist went to Newcastle to fetch 
it, and provided a waggon for it.3 


The floor of the choir appears to have been strewn 
with rushes, and the rushes for this and other floors 
were brought on the backs of horses, in great part at 
least, from the marshes near Stockton, where the Abbey 
held the manor of Bewley and a large estate. 

The remote ancestors of the present jackdaws seem 
to have given trouble to the Sacrist, who had some 
difficulty in excluding them from the interior of the 
church.4 


We occasionally find mention of goldleaf and colours 
for pictures and images, and of linseed oil for paint. 


Lenten preachers were brought over then as now; 
at that time they were usually preaching friars from 
Newcastle, and they were feasted on a Lenten repast

Each of the principal officers had his pittance or

He went into the Infirmary, and was supplied with

The funds for carrying on all the business in the hands 
of the Sacrist came principally from the estate now called 
Sacristonheugh,3 often named in the Rolls ‘le Hough,” or 
Chvus Sacriste. It was and is still a large farm, about 
four miles N.W. of Durham, and there are some small 
portions of the medieval house yet remaining. ‘‘ The 
house is built on the crest of an almost precipitous hill,” 
and ‘‘is now divided into tenements. The oldest portions 
are of thirteenth-century date, and comprise a pointed 
doorway with characteristic moulding on arch and 
_ jambs, a round-headed doorway of plainer character, 
a shouldered doorway now walled up, and a low 
barrel-vaulted apartment. There is a curious little two- 
light window of fifteenth-century date, both lights trefoil- 
headed, and cut in a single stone. Part of an ancient 
stone staircase still exists. The whole building, though 
much altered, is very picturesque. A huge stack of 
chimneys rises from the middle of the roofs, and what 
appears to be a massive buttress on the south front is 
really the projecting shaft of a gardrobe, but the entrance 
is now closed."4 The Sacrist managed the estate with the

THE FERETRAR., 


A good many of the Feretrars’ rolls have been 
preserved.3 We have seen above that at the time 
of the Dissolution the offices of Master of the Feretory 
and Deece Prior were held by the same person, and in 
Rites we have an account of his duties in both capacities. 
He kept the keys of the shrine, and delivered them to 
the clerk of the Feretory when any man of honour or 
worship requested to have it opened, and also in Matins 
time when Ze Deum was sung, or in the High Mass time, 
or at Evensong during the Magnificat. The master stood 
by to see the cover of the shrine drawn up, and to receive 
back the keys from the clerk when it was closed. No 
doubt he also superintended the opening and closing of 
the almeries in which the relics were kept.4 And when 
any valuable offerings were made, he saw that they were 
hung on the shrine by means of the silver hooks that are 
mentioned in the Rolls. He also had charge of the 
famous banner of St. Cuthbert, which was ordinarily 
‘kept with the shrine. When it was borne in processions, 
or taken away to a battle-field, it was. the office of the 
clerk of the Feretory to attend to it, ‘‘ with his surplice 
on.”5 The clerk is frequently mentioned$; in 1386-87 he 
was sent to Oxford, and we find in the Feretrar’s inventory 
_of 1441-42 a surplice for the clerk. In 1480-81 nine ells of 
linen were bought for the clerk’s surplice, which, with the 
making, cost 4s. 104d. We find mention of vestments

THE VICARS. 


The Bursar, the Cellarer, the Chamberlain, the 
Hostillar, the Master of the Garners, and the Sacrist, 
all had their vicarit tn ecclesia,s3 who appear to have 
taken their places in the church when they were 
‘‘reasonably let or hindered” from attending in consequence 
of their official engagements or otherwise. The remunera- 
tion in all cases was 6s. 8d. a year, which payments 
appear among the Exfense Necessarie or the Dona et 
Exennia, not among the regular Stipendia.

INTRODUCTION. XXill 


We now come to the second class of officers, namely 
those of the monastery as distinct from those of the Prior’s 
household and those concerned in Divine Service. The 
chief among these was the Bursar. 


THE BURSAR. 


According to Az¢es, the Bursar received all the rents 
pertaining to the house, and all other officers of the 
house made out their accounts to him. He paid the 
servants’ wages, and all the expenses that the house was 
charged with. His checker was a little stone house joining 
the coal garth belonging to the great kitchen, near the 
Prior’s, now the Dean’s, hall stairs. His chamber was in 
the Infirmary, and his meat was served from the great 
kitchen to his checker.* 

The Bursars’ Rolls are far greater in bulk and number 
than any of the others, and the extracts from these alone 
form nearly one-third of those contained in the present 
volumes.? The Rolls become gradually longer as time goes 
on, and that of 1536-37, which is printed zz extenso, is 
16% feet long, and as printed occupies 41 pages.3 Of 
these more than half contain the receipts arranged under 
the various places from which rents and tithes came, and 
then follow the expenses under their various heads. We 
should expect from what is stated in Az¢es that the Bursars’ 
Rolls would simply be extracts from those of the other 
officers, but such is not the case. They may have rendered 
their accounts to him, and their receipts and spendings 
may have passed through his hands, but he kept an 
account of his own independent of the rest, and concerned 
with many different matters. The amount and variety of 
their contents is such that I find it impossible to deal with 
them in the same way as I am doing with the other Rolls. 
I can only refer to some of the most remarkable matters, 
and to the Index, which, under some heads, gives a good 
many particulars, all of which from page 484 to page 707 are 
in the Bursars’ Rolls. See, for instance, Abbey, Bishop, 
Bursar, Coal mines, Cuthbert, Durham, Friars, Gloves, 
Horses, King, etc., Mazers, Oxford, Pannus, Pixes,

There are several references in the Bursars’ Rolls (and 
a few in those of the Cellarers) to the visits to Durham of 
royal personages, chiefly if not entirely in connexion with 
the Scotch wars. At different times we meet with Edward 
II, Edward III, and Henry IV, sometimes with the Queen 
Consort, and always witha retinue of courtiers and servants, 
requiring not only to be boarded and lodged in royal style, 
but to receive instead of making ceremonial presents. 


* In p. 707, line 11, for 531, read 631. 


INTRODUCTION. XXV 


Many of these will be found under the head Dona et 
Exennia. Sometimes the king’s officers received presents 
on the express understanding that they should keep their 
men and horses off the standing corn and hay crops of 
the monastery, and it has been already mentioned how 
the wood cart had to be kept out of their way. On 
one occasion a servant of the queen was paid 25. to 
save the cheese at Beaurepaire.!. The king of Scotland 
appears to have been in Durham c7rca 1335, for there is 
mention of provender and of drugs for his horses, and of 
his messengers, his garciones, and his histriones. The 
same followers are frequently named in connexion with the 
king of England, who was also, as we have seen, usually 
attended by his ‘‘ fool.” Edward III had a cook with him 
in 1333-34, and, in 1335-36, pants dominicus and simnel 
_ were provided for the king and queen “et aliis super- 
venientibus ”’ on the way northward, when the banner of 
St. Cuthbert was taken with the king to Scotland. In that 
word ‘‘supervenientibus ” we have, perhaps, a hint as to 
one light in which these royal visits were regarded. 
Among the Expense Necessarie of 1300-01 are, for a 
present made to the king on his arrival, 69s. 6d. ; to the 
lord de Vescy, tos. 6d. ; and to the queen, 21s.; and at 
other times we find valuable presents of horses, a chariot, 
hounds, etc., made by the Prior and Convent to the king. 
In 1335-36 we find a charge of 8d. for one gallon of wine 
bought for a certain horse of our lady the queen, but 
whether the wine was employed to comfort the heart of the 
animal or that of the royal palfrey-man may perhaps admit 
of some doubt: The banner of St. Cuthbert was carried 
into Scotland, or in that direction, about a dozen times at 
least, and together with it a tent for its protection and that 
of its bearer. In 1400 it was with Henry IV at Holy 
Island, where the king appears to have been lodged. The 
last recorded occasion is that of the battle of Flodden, of 
which there is an interesting notice, in which the English 
victory is said to have been ‘‘ Dei adjutorio,” ‘‘ assistente

In 1333-34 we find some interesting notices of the 
unhappy episode of the election and consecration of Bishop 
de Graystanes, and the forcing upon the Convent by the 
king of his former tutor, Richard de Bury, at the earnest 
entreaty of the queen. There are the expenses of the Prior 
meeting Bishop Robert de Graystanes at Ketton about 
his consecration, and at Beaurepaire for three weeks when 
the same bishop came thither. Then the expenses of the 
Prior when he went to York to confer with the rival 
bishop, Richard de Bury, and when he had to entertain 
Bishop Richard at Ketton. In a separate paragraph we 
have expenses of Bishop de Graystanes paid by the 
convent, viz., wine at his installation ; two friends going 
to York for the consecration; his going to and from the 
king and Bishop de Bury at Ketton four times, no doubt 
to plead his righteous cause ; his expenses at Beaurepaire 
when he last returned from the south ; housings of his 
horses : shoeing of his palfrey ; and money advanced for 
his expenses. Graystanes was Sub-Prior of Durham, one 
of the historians of the church, and a man whose character 
won for him the kindly respect of the supporters of his 
rival. In his own account of the matter he affords an 
example of high-minded resignation to the inevitable, not 
without something of natural and reasonable disappoint- 
ment. When he died he was laid to rest with the other 
bishops in the Chapter-house, and fortunately his inscribed 
grave-slab is one of those which have escaped destruction. 
It bears the inscription

Among names of Newcastle merchants that occur is 
that of the famous Roger Thornton ; his name appears no 
less than seventeen times.2 Wine, wax, planks, lead, 
and Spanish iron were bought of him again and again ; 
in 1401-02 the Sacrist borrowed from him £10 13s. 6d., 
and in 1407-09 a pipe of Rumney was bought of him 
for 100s., of which he condoned to the lord Prior 8os.,

If the reader will look up the matters to which I have

whole of the extracts, which is really the only way to

THE TERRAR. 


This officer must originally have had to look after 
the landed estates and their produce, but afterwards 
that duty seems to have devolved mainly on the Bursar, 
the Keeper of the Garners,! and the various officers resident 
at the manors, etc. He appears at the time of the Disso- 
lution simply as guest-master,? nevertheless there were 
hostillars up to that time, many of whose rolls are 
preserved, though the hostillars are not mentioned among 
the officers of the abbey in the fiftieth chapter of Aztes. The 
Terrars’ Rolls are very short, and deal with an income and 
expenditure rarely exceeding £30. The former was derived 
from the dvasinagiwm and other customary payments from 
certain places, as Cornage, Elsilver, Averpennies, Metred, 
and Cartsilver. The expenses are of a very miscellaneous 
character, and include some curious particulars, as con- 
tributions towards the maintenance of the sheep-farm at 
the Holme; 20d. to the cooks on Easter Day ; a saddle 
for the Terrar, and 2s. to his laundress; 5s. to the 
Coroner for a son of John Shepherd who was drowned, 
and half a quarter of barley given to the said John; 
togas for clericult, and liberatura (probably the same) for 
five puert ecclesie against Christmas, 20s. for the paving 
in the choir at Northallerton, 6s. 8d. and 13s. 6d. for the 
making of a caroll in the cloister, 6s. 6d. for the making 
of a bridge at the Holme, mending and making of road 
and ways, much mustard seed bought, irons for marking 
animals, 6s. 8d. to the bishop’s chaplain celebrating his 
first mass, two gold rings given to the wives of two 
gentlemen, one of whom sent venison to the Prior the 
same year, three pair of calige given’to the servants of 
the other, repair of gate of new bridge in Durham, expenses

#156 58. 4% d., leaving a balance of 201 3520570

The Cellarer provided the food required for the guests,

as a rule, be habitual observers of Lent in the matter of 
diet. 

THE CELLARER. 


This important officer is one of the few that are 
named in the Benedictine Rule. At Durham, his office 
appears to have always been as it is partly described 
in A7zfes,2 namely, to see what flesh-meat was required 
in the kitchen in each week, and what spices ‘and 
other necessaries” were used, both for the Prior’s 
table and for the whole Convent, and for all strangers that 
came. The term ‘‘other necessaries” admits of a wide 
application, including, as it does, fish and fowl, and many 
other things; as may be expected, it receives large 
illustration from the Rolls, and, as to the ‘‘strangers,” we 
have already seen that they were not provided for by the 
Hostillar, except in the matter of certain luxuries which

XXXIV INTRODUCTION. 


were not to be had from the kitchen. It is expressly 
mentioned that it was the Cellarer’s office to see all things 
orderly served and in due time. In this duty he was 
assisted by a subordinate officer called the Refectorarius. 
His checker was at the top of some steps, now destroyed, on 
the west side of the Great Kitchen, and his chamber was 
in the dormitory. 

There are Cellarers’ Rolls from 1307 to 1535, and in 
dealing with them we are met by the same difficulty as that 
which is connected with the Bursars’ Rolls, namely the 
great amount and variety of material contained in them. 
The accounts seem to have been kept in different ways at 
different times, and so there is some variety in the form of 
the rolls. In the earlier rolls we have the expenses entered 
by the week and month, as in 1333-34, but in the earliest 
extant roll, that for 1307-08, the weekly sums only are 
entered, without the particulars. In that year the total 
receipts of the Cellarer are stated at £442 3s. 10d., of 
which sum £401 was received from the Bursar, by tally. 
The roll of 1438-39 is the first extant of another series 
described on page 62. There are interesting inventories of 
goods in charge of the Cellarer in 1459 and 1480. Of fish 
and other sea creatures used for food, there are named no 
less than 65 kinds; of flesh, including portions of animals, 
21; of fowl, 27; of fruit, 9; of spices, 15; of what we 
should call ‘‘ groceries,” 17; besides sundries, such as 
candle-wick, bolt-cloths, canvas for strainers and aprons, 
charcoal for the kitchen, packthread, marking-irons for 
vessels and for beasts, scales and troy weights, keslops, 
butter and cheese for flawns, pork for froys, butter-cups, a 
spade for cutting hay, etc. Among buildings named are 
the salthouse, the slaughter-house, the pastehouse, the 
goosehouse, the seething-house, the roasting-range, the 
brewhouse, the apple-house, the dovecote, and the capon- 
house. Among persons employed: women fetching 
water, gathering moss, and carrying paving-stones, the 
ratoner and the ferreter, the cellarer’s servants generally.? 
Among occupations, lighting the cressets in the chapter-

THE ALMONER. 


This officer is not one of those who are named in 
Rites, where, however, the children of the Almery, 
the care of whom was one of his duties, are frequently 
referred to. His principal duties were in connexion 
with the Manor and Hospital at Witton Gilbert and 
the Hospital of St. Mary Magdalene at Durham, 
with the estates connected with them, which he appears 
to have kept in his own hands, also of the Infirmary with- 
out the Gates between the North and the South Bailey in 
Durham. Such were the methods by which the monastic 
almoners in the middle ages discharged their duties to the 
poor, rather than by such personal attendance on them at 
their own homes as is enjoined in Lanfranc’s constitutions. 3 
But no doubt the sick and infirm were much better tended 
in the hospitals than they could have been at home. 

The Hospital at Witton Gilbert was founded during 
the reign of Bishop Pudsey by Gilbert de la Ley, the lord 
of Witton, asa hospital for five lepers. Surtees prints the 
original charters,s which are in the Treasury. The

The hospital stood at a short distance from the church, 
and parts of it may have been worked into the present farm 
house. A pointed window built in is said to have been 
brought from Bearpark. 

No distinct account of the origin of the Hospital of 
St. Mary Magdalene or of the rectory attached to it has 
been found. What is known may be seen in the Intro- 
duction to Memorials of St. Giles’s, xxix—xxxiii. The 
second, if not the third, church or chapel is still standing in 
a ruined state in a garden to the north of Gilesgate in 
Durham. There is a short notice of it, with a ground- 
plan, in Vol. ii of the Durham Archeological Transactions, 
where are translations of the passages in the almoners’ 
rolls concerning the pulling down of the former church 
and the building of the present ruined church on a better 
site in the immediate neighbourhood. For this removal 
the Prior and Convent obtained a licence from Bishop 
Neville, in which the chapel is described as a parish church 
annexed to the office of almoner in the Cathedral Church.? 
There is a small view of the present ruin in the foreground 
of the general view of Durham from the N.E. in the 
supplementary plates in Billings’s County of Durham, 
Pl. I. The ‘‘reticulated” tracery of the east window 
there shown has fallen out, and the Frosterley marble 
step of the font (p. 240) recovered by Mr. Thompson3 has 
_ again disappeared.

Concerning the Infirmary a the Abbey gates we 
have some information in ARztes. It was founded by the 
Prior and Convent at some time unknown, and was main- 
tained at their cost. ‘There was a school in this Infirmary, 
where the children of the Almery were daily fed and taught 
by the schoolmaster, who was a priest, and said mass in 
the chapel of this Infirmary on every holy day and Friday, 
at Magdalen’s chapel twice, and at Kimblesworth chapel 
once a week. Besides the children of the Almery, who 
seem to have gone to their own homes to sleep, there were 
four aged women who lived altogether in the Infirmary, 
having each a separate chamber to sleep in, and being fed 
with what came from the Prior’s own table. Whenever 
‘‘the Infirmary” is mentioned in the Almoners’ rolls, it 
is this one that is usually meant, and not the monastic 
Infirmary within the gates. 

The Roll of 1428-29 seems to show that there were 28 
out-brethren and sisters at that time, and eight living in 
the Infirmary, so that by the time of the Dissolution it 
must have fallen into considerable decay, if it maintained 
only the ‘‘1iij°’ ould womenne” and the children of the 
Almery remembered by the author of Rites. In 1439-40 
and in some years next preceding we find 28 brethren 
‘cum famula eorundem,” but these 28 cannot all have 
been living in the house together. Perhaps they ‘‘ came 
into residence” in turn. There is a building-account of 
this Infirmary and its chapel in 1372-73, and as it is

sometimes called ‘‘the Infirmary between the two Baileys” 
its site can be identified exactly ; it must have stood where 
some coach-houses or the adjoining houses opposite to the 
Abbey gates now are. 

We find in the Rolls that the bell of the Infirmary 
without the gates was repaired, and that for the chapel of 
either this Infirmary or the other a surplice and fringe for 
a vestment were procured.! In 1401-02 we find mention of 
a corporal, and in 1465 of a chalice in a leathern case. 
Bupein the Status of 1472 under the head Casella 
Infirmarie we have a list of 24 articles belonging thereto, 
and under other heads a very complete list of all the 
articles in charge of the Almoner. 

The Almoner would be considerably occupied by the 
charge of the three establishments assigned to his office, 
and accordingly we find that he, like some other of his 
brethren, had a Vicar in the Church. 

There are Almoners’ Rolls extant from 1312 to 1527, 
and among them will be found, in whole or in part, no less 
than fifteen inventories of stock at Durham, Witton, 
Rookhopschele in Weardale, where the Almoner had a 
farm and iron-mines, and St. Mary Magdalene’s. These 
inventories include not only farm stock and implements, 
but some household and church goods. We also have 
accounts of the building of the church or chapel of St. 
Mary Magdalene in 1370, of the building of the Infirmary 
without the gates, and of its chapel3 in 1372, and very full 
particulars of the rebuilding on another site of St. Mary 
-Magdalene’s chapel in 1449-50. In the accounts next 
following we have the fitting with stalls, the stocking of 
the bell, the step for the font, and the dedication of the 
church, altar, and churchyard by the bishop suffragan, 
May 16, 1451. 

The Almoners’ Rolls do not furnish us with so many 
curious details as do some of the others. The receipts are 
mainly from rents of houses and lands in the city and

THE COMMONER. 


The duties of this officer were not very arduous. 
According to /eztes,? his office was to provide figs and 
walnuts and also such spices against Lent as should 
be comfortable for the monks in a time of great austerity 
both of fasting and of praying, to keep up a good 
fire in the Common-house hall, and to have by him a 
hogshead of wine for the monks and for the keeping of his 
‘‘O” or annual pittance on the day called ‘‘O Sapientia,”’3 
which, as we are told, ‘‘the Prior and Covent dyd use at 
that tyme of the yere onely,” so that there seems to have 
been something exceptional about it. It may perhaps be 
referred to in 1511-12 as ‘‘una cena noviter facta confra- 
tribus.”4 This ‘‘sollemne banquett” is delightfully de- 
scribed in Aztes, ch. xlv. There we learn that the Common- 
house was in a part of the undercroft of the dormitory, 
namely on the right as they passed through from the 
cloisters to the Infirmary beyond. Also that the Common- 
house had a garden and a bowling-alley at the back, for 
the recreation of the monks and novices; the space 
formerly occupied by these is now a lawn, sometimes used 
as a bowling-green. At the door of the Common-house 
was a lantern, which was repaired in 1312-13, at the 
expense of the Cellarer.s The floor was strewn with 
rushes. 

There are Commoners’ Rolls from 1416 to 1535.7 
The first of these is the account of William Graystanes 
and John Tynemouth, who appear to have held office 
conjointly, unless there was a change during the year. 
The receipts besides ‘‘arrears” (balance to the good) 
viz., those of 31 years’ accounts, and other arrears, 
were £69 158. 44d. ; with arrears, £903 3s. 84d. The

expenses were 471 11s. 9%d. In 1524-25 the receipts 
were £114 18s. 93¢d., and the expenses £04 12s. 11d. 
The income was derived from rents of tenements 
and lands in the city and county, and from the endow- 
ments of the Neville, Fossor, Skirlaugh, and Rudd 
chantries, from part of the tithes of Bywell St. 
Peter, of Hett, and of certain coal mines, pensions 
from a few churches and religious houses, profits of the 
court and toll-hall of Hett, sale of oak bark and tops, ete. 
The expenses were for quarterly payments to the brethren, 
purchase of spices, pensions and stipends to the Precentor, 
Succentor, Master of the Infirmary, the Commoner himself, 
and the chantry-priests, with some smaller payments, 
presents (including gloves), redditus resoluti, necessary 
expenses for coal and firewood, white candles, and other 
charges of the usual kind. The Common-house must 
have been very dark during a great part of the year, hence 
the need for the large quantity of candles that were used, 
as well as great torches on some occasions. 

There are, of course, the usual charges for building 
materials for the maintenance of the tenements that were 
assigned to the Commoner. The most characteristic of the 
expenses are those for spices, fuel, and candles for the 
Common-house. There is a very good inventory of 1517,? 
which enables us to re-furnish the Common-house in 
imagination with its tables, seats, towels, napkins, plate, 
spice platters and boxes, wooden dishes for figs, candle- 
boxes, almery, etc. The czmba monachorum, kept at the 
‘‘ boatstead,”? with two oars, and a lock, key, and chain, 
was in charge of the Commoner, and it often wanted 
repairing. It appears that he had a storehouse in Cross- 
gate for building materials3 and a coalpit at Hett.4 At 
the end of this inventory is a list of brewleads and other 
brewing apparatus at a number of houses in Durham, the 
tenants of which evidently brewed at their own homes. 

Minor ailments seem to have been attended to by the 
Commoner, for we find frequent mention of electuary for 
the monks and novices, commonly called ‘‘lettorye.”

limited in its connotation than it formerly was, though in 
dialect use it still means any kind of sweetmeats, spice- 
cake is “plum” or currant cake, and a spice-shop is a 
shop where children’s sweets are sold. 


THE MASTER OF THE INFIRMARY. 


There is very little about the Infirmary in the chapter 
concerning it in Azées,3 and the Master is only incidentally 
mentioned. What is there said is limited to the Lying- 
house, a strong prison that was under the Master’s 
chamber. There is more about the Infirmary itself 
in the chapters on the burying of monks and of 
Priors.4 There we learn that a sick man might have 
both fire and more convenient keeping in the Infirmary 
than in the dormitory, where no fire was allowed. And 
when he died and had been wound in his cowl and 
habit he was carried into a room in the Infirmary called 
the ‘‘ Dead man’s chamber.” The door of the chamber 
where he died was locked, and the key taken to the 
Prior. At night he was removed from the Dead man’s 
chamber to St. Andrew’s chapel, adjoining the said 
chamber and the Infirmary. During the night two monks 
remained on their knees at his feet, and the children of 
the Almery knelt in the stalls on either side reciting the

Psalter. In the morning the corpse was carried first to 
the Chapter house for the Dirige and then to the Centry 
garth for burial. We should have welcomed some account 
of the management of the sick in the Infirmary, but /z/es 
is. silent on that subject. 

The Rolls of the Masters of the Infirmary are very 
short, and the receipts and expenses are mostly under 
410. Nevertheless they contain a good many interesting 
particulars. They range in date from 1352 to 1535.1 The 
receipts are some small rents, and contributions from some 
other officers. The expenses are for a pittance on St. 
Andrew’s day, repairs of the Infirmary buildings, coal 
and wood for fuel, candles, servants’ wages, linen, rushes 
for the floors, etc.2 The annual pittance seems to have 
been one of the ‘‘moderate and_ scholastical”’ order,3 
similar to the Commoner’s ‘‘O.” The Infirmary chapel 
was dedicated in honour of St. Andrew, it had a great east 
window, and an east door with a pavement before it,4 a 
west window, a picture over the altar, figures of St. Andrew 
and others, stalls, etc. In the Bursar’s roll of 1353-54 is 
the entry, ‘‘In fenestris vitreis cancelli Infirmariz 
reparandis, 4s.” The ‘‘ great window” of the chapel 
had 38 feet of new glass put into it in 1467-68 and 20 feet 
in 1469-70, at 10d. a foot. A Lenten veil with red crosses 
on it, and a frontal for the altar, ‘‘ejusdem secte,” were 
made of seven ells of Holland cloth in 1448-49. The site 
of St. Andrew’s chapel is no longer to be identified. 
Search for its foundations was made some years ago with- 
out any positive result.

It should be pointed out that the Infirmary was not 
for the sick alone ; a few of the older monks, bowed down 
by age and sometimes by chronic ailments as well, and no 
longer able to bear their part in the daily life and the long 
and frequent religious offices of a monastery, took up their 
abode permanently in the Infirmary, which at Westminster 
was converted for them into a little quadrangle of separate

THE INSTAURARIUS OR INSTAURATOR. 


This officer exercised a general supervision of the 
live-stock of the monastery, and of the Bercarii, Vaccarii, 
Stirkettarii, Bovettarii, Stodardi, and Custodes, at the 
various manors and farms. There are rolls of /nstaurari 
and of their subordinates from 1338 to 1482.4 — 

Some of these are accounts of receipts and expenses, 
others inventories of stock. The receipts are from sales 
of cattle, etc., as shown on page 309, the expenses for 
purchases of stock, implements, etc., construction and 
repairs of buildings, furnishing of dairies, payment of 


wages, etc. One curious thing that the Rolls show is, the 
frequent sale of hides and carcases of animals that had died 


in murrain; even the Cellarer bought carcases of that 
description. The flesh of a cow that had so died was “ of 
no value,” not on that account, but because it was putrid ; 
nevertheless the hide was sold for 8a.5 Some sheep are 


accounted for as having been devoured by dogs or by

Among labours mentioned are, sheepwashing and 
salving, hedging and ditching, mowing, reaping, and hay- 
making, getting meadow-thatch, thatching stacks with

The stock-keepers suffered with the rest of the officers 
in the Scotch wars, and that from both of the contending 
parties. Stock had to be driven south of Tees,3 and 
some were lost, through fear of the Scots,4 while lambs

THE SUPERVISOR EQUICII. 


This officer has been referred to above in connexion 
with the Prior’s household," but his being called Supervisor 
Equici Priorts*t probably means no more than that he 
served the Prior as head of the monastery and not as the 
master of a separate household. He is not mentioned in 
fites, and there is only one remaining roll pertaining to 
his office, namely that of 1420-21. This roll hardly 
requires any separate notice here, it speaks for itself.

THE GRANATORIUS. 


This officer is described in Aztest as Keeper or Master 
of the Garners. He had a checker in the Garners, where 
the wheat and other corn lay. He kept an account of 
the wheat and malt corn as they came in and were 
expended. The malt kiln was in connexion with the 
garners, which after the Dissolution were converted into 
the prebendal houses in the middle of the south side of 
the College. These buildings, besides their outside walls, 
retain some ancient features. The chamber of the Master 
of the Garners was in the Dormitory. 

When the extracts that form the bulk of these volumes 
were made in the first instance, the Granators’ Rolls were 
passed by as of less interest. A recent examination of 
some of them has shown that their contents are of consider- 
ably more importance than was then supposed, and it may 
be worth while to give some account of them, with extracts, 
in this place. 

There are 111 of them in all, ranging from 1296 ? to 
1533. The one dated 1296 on the wrapper is much decayed 
and mouse-eaten, and the date is now gone, all but 
‘<> sexto.” Its contents are of the same kind as those 
of the later ones, but it is too much decayed to afford any 
connected information. In the Roll of 1341-42 we find 
that among the corn dispensed extra curiam, the Almoner 
received by tally g quarters and 5 bushels. Several 
servants at different places received allowances of wheat, 
and presents were made ex precepio Priorts, or wheat was 
given in exchange for or else as food for poultry, thus, 
‘‘Coco Prioris pro pull. gallin. j pe. Gardinario Prioris

THE MASTER OF THE NOVICES. 


Besides a full account in Rites,* there are several 
incidental notices of this officer in that record. There were 


‘Che xix: 


INTRODUCTION. Ilvil 


always six novices,t who went daily to their books within 
the cloister? for seven years. Their master was one of the 
oldest monks, whose duty was not only to instruct them in 
learning, but to exercise a general care over them, and to 
apply to the Chamberlain for any clothes that they required. 
He took his meals with them in the Frater house.3 If any 
of them showed themselves specially apt to learn, they were 
sent to Durham College in Oxford, and the residue were 
kept at their books till they could understand their service 
and the Scriptures. Then they were ordained priests and 
sang their first mass and received black tunics.4 After 
this the House no longer found them apparel, but gave 
them 20s. a year to find themselves, unless they held some 
office that could afford it, and then they had extra garments, 
as we often find in the Rolls. The master’s chamber was 

in the Dormitory. As he had no accounts to keep, there 
are no rolls belonging to his office; both he and his pupils, 
however, frequently come before us in the rolls of the 
Chamberlain and other officers. 


CHAPLAINS OR CHANTRY PRIESTS. 


These are frequently mentioned in the Rolls, in which 
occur references to the chantries of the lords Neville, of 
the Bishops and Richard of Barnard Castle, of Bishop 
Skirlaugh, of Prior Fossor, of Prior Castell, of John 
Rude and of Robert and Agnes Rodd’, both names 
probably being the same, and of Isabel Lawson. None 
of these were chantries of separate foundation, so far 
as I can ascertain, but were arrangements made by the 
Prior and Convent to provide for masses for certain persons 
in return for benefactions to the church. These masses 
were probably at first said by the monks, but we find that 
in 1536 four chantry-priests received from the Bursar gos. 
‘each for the year. These may or may not have been

south aisle of the nave, and the Neville tombs now placed

taken their place. We know something about the origin 
of the Neville chantry from Chambre, who informs us that 
in 1355 Ralph lord Neville assigned to the Common House 
an annual rent of 1o/.3 that a monk, celebrating daily for 
whom he would, might remember the souls of himself and 
his wife and all the faithful departed. This annual pay- 
ment was afterwards compounded for by John lord Neville, 
son of the above-named Ralph, who released the Prior and 
Convent from a debt of 4oo/. which they owed him.s5 The

Prior Fossor, a great benefactor, ordained, with the 
consent of the chapter, that a monk should say a mass for 
_his soul each day at the altar of St. Nicholas and St. Giles 
in the north transept, and for this purpose, and for a 
pittance on his anniversary, he assigned to the common- 
house lands and rents. Two rentals of the chantries of 
Walter Skyrley (Bishop Skirlaw) and John Fossor are 
mentioned in a Commoner’s Inventory of 1517, page 293. 

In 1524 the Commoner paid the Succentor 6s. 8d. for 
the ¢abulacio of Fossor’s chantry. And in the same year 
he received rents for the chantries of Fossor, Skyrley, and 
John Rude. Prior Fossor was buried before the altar at 
which mass was said for him.?

Ixii INTRODUCTION. 


Prior Castell bought two mills, commonly called 
Jesus mills, covered them with lead, and granted them to 
the Church of Durham, in order that after his death there 
might be a memorial of him in the mass of Jesus, and he 
was buried in front of the Jesus altar at the east end of the 
nave.t’ The Sacrist’s Roll of 1535-36 mentions fines and 
rents from the Jesus mill as assigned to the office of Sacrist 
by Thomas Castell, ‘‘ pro cantaria Nominis Jha.” 

The chantry of John Rude, mentioned above in 
connexion with that of Prior Fossor, was probably the 
same as that of Robert Rodd’ and Agnes Rodd’. For a 
payment to their chantry priests, see page 704. That is 
all that I have noted about them or their chantry, though 
no doubt the payment occurs year by year. The celebrant 
for John Rudde received from the Commoner 48s. in 1524.3 

Robert and Agnes may have augmented an earlier 
endowment. The former of these may have been the 
famous Robert Rodes of Newcastle, who was the originator 
of St. Nicholas’ Steeple in that town, and is described in 
the Rolls as a constant and faithful friend of St. Cuthbert, 
and who presented to the shrine a magnificent cross of gold 
and jewels, and was a great benefactor to the church in 
many ways.4 

Concerning the chantry of Isabel Lawson I have met 
with nothing in the Rolls or elsewhere except the notice 
of itin the Sacrist’s Roll of 1536, page 418. One Isabel 
Lawson who is mentioned, with many others of the same 
name, in Durham Wills, Vol. Il, was twice married, and 
seems to have lived too late to have founded a chantry,5 but 
something of the kind was probably done by an earlier 
lady in the same family. 

The above-named are all the chantries concerning 
which I have noted anything in the Rolls. Any one 
going through them with that special object might 
no doubt find more about them, or might find references 
to some which I have missed. The most important

chantry in the church, that founded by Bishop Langley

Besides the chantries, there was the Guild of St. 
Cuthbert in the Galilee,3 apparently a brotherhood mention- 
ed in the Sacrists’ Rolls as ‘‘ Fraeria S. Cuthberti.” In 
the 11th year of Bishop Neville, 1448-49, John Lound, 
clerk, William Raket, Robert Rhodes, Richard Raket, 
Robert Sotheron, chaplain, and John Bynchestre, chaplain, 
had a ‘‘licence to establish a Gild to the honour of St. 
Cuthbert, in the chapel of the blessed Mary, within the 
Galilee of the monastery of Durham.’4 The Fraeria, 
however, existed much earlier. It may, perhaps, have 
been established on some new footing in 1448-49. It 
appears to have had on its roll persons in Northumberland 
and Hexhamshire as well as in the Bishopric.5 But I 
know nothing further concerning it. 


This Introduction has now run to a length which may, 
perhaps, be considered excessive. But my object has been 
to give a pretty full general account of the contents of the 
Rolls and of some matters connected therewith. This
