will, I hope, be acceptable to some of our members who 
have neither the time nor the inclination to go through the 
original matter. I may perhaps here say a few words 
about the Index and Glossary. I have tried to omit 
nothing in the Index. But as the compilation of it 
extended over some years, I am afraid that, after all the 
revision I have bestowed on it, some references which 
ought to have been brought together are distributed under 
two or more synonymous words, and that more cross- 
references might have been given with advantage. I have 
tried to make it to some extent a subject-index. That it is 
not more complete in this respect is of less consequence, 
because of the lists of things mentioned in the Rolls that 
will be found at the end of this Introduction, the idea of 
which I took from the lists at the end of the great Lexicon 
of Du Cange. The Index may be referred to for any of 
the things mentioned in the lists, and I hope it will not 
often be referred to in vain. The Glossary has grown 
considerably in my hands. At first I thought of giving 
only a list of obscure words, with short explanations - 
when known. But I hope that the fuller treatment ulti- 
mately adopted will meet with approval. The number of 
curious words in the Rolls is very great indeed, and I 
cannot say how many hundred quotations I have sent to 
Dr. Murray for the New English Dictionary. With 
reference to these, Dr. Murray has very kindly sent me © 
the following interesting remarks for publication here. 
‘¢The Account Rolls,” he says, ‘‘are of immense value in 
enlarging our knowledge of the English Vocabulary of the 
Fourteenth, Fifteenth, and early Sixteenth centuries ; and, 
in issuing them, the Surtees Society has done an impor- 
tant service to English lexicography. Every one who 
tries to gather the vocabulary of any past age from its 
surviving monuments knows how difficult it is to recover 
the words that lie out of the track of ordinary literature, 
which do not naturally occur in the chronicles, histories, 
religious treatises, ballad or lyric poetry of the time. 
From these sources we gather without difficulty the names 
of persons and things of general interest, the ordinary 
adjectives and verbs, the pronouns, the particles, which 


INTRODUCTION. Ixv 


enter into the substance or frame-work of all written 
language. But the names of articles of domestic use, of 
the materials and tools of the artificer and artisan, of the 
specific parts of buildings, offices, and furniture, rarely— 
in many cases never—appear in literature, and would be 
entirely lost to us, but for their preservation in two sources, 
viz., in vocabularies, nominalia, or glossaries, Latin- 
English or English-Latin, in which they are arranged 
usually under subject-headings, which the compiler has 
evidently tried to make reasonably complete, and in such 
private records as the Account Rolls here edited and made 
accessible, in which English words, in their vernacular 
form, or with mere latinized endings, occur in a Latin 
context. Each of these sources has its points of advantage. 
The words in the Vocabulary are furnished with a Latin 
explanation, which usually (but by no means always) 
makes the meaning intelligible. In the Accounts the 
words are not explained, but they occur in a natural 
context, which sometimes indeed leaves their sense 
undetermined, but often determines it more satisfactorily 
than the Latin equivalent in the vocabulary. But in one 
respect these Durham Accounts have the advantage of all 
our English-Latin vocabularies : the latter rarely go back 
into the Fourteenth century. The Fifteenth century (as I 
have pointed out in my Romanes Lecture) was the age of 
the renascence of English lexicography, in which the 
making of native English glossaries and vocabularies 
(which had come to an end with the Norman Conquest) 
burst anew into activity. With the Fifteenth century, 
therefore, the history of an immense number of words of 
the non-literary or less literary side of the language begins. 
Now, the publication of these Accounts, which go back 
more than a century earlier, carries back into that century 
the evidence for the existence and form of a large number 
of words, of which they now supply the earliest-known 
Middle English instances. Hence their publication has 
proved of high importance to the new English Dictionary, 
few pages of which are now without a quotation from them, 
which in many cases is moreover our earliest evidence for 
the word, or fills up a lacuna in its history between the 


ee 


Ixvi INTRODUCTION. 


Old English or Anglo-Saxon period and the Fifteenth 
century.” 

In turn, I must here acknowledge the great help 
I have received from the ‘‘N.E.D.” in the preparation 
of the Glossary, so far as the Dictionary has advanced. 
I have usually found it more helpful than any other source 
of information to which I have turned. | 

As will be seen, there are still a good many words 
awaiting explanation after I have done all in my power, 
but without success, to elucidate them. 

As I hear of many enquiries as to when the new 
edition of Aztes of Durham may be expected to appear, 
I may say that as soon as this volume is off my hands 
I hope to add to the notes collected some years ago a great 
number of references to the Account Rolls, and to give a 
general revision to the whole of the old notes. And I do 
not see why this should not be done in the course of the 
present year. 


I have now only to add the expression of my best 
thanks to all the kind friends who have helped me in 
various ways in connexion with these volumes. And 
first, the Dean and Chapter of Durham, who have so long 
allowed me free access to the Rolls and other manuscripts 
contained in their Treasury, and for the generous help to 
the Surtees Society that is referred to in the Preface to 
Vol. II. Next, to the Dean, for his never-failing sympathy 
and his most valuable help with the proof-sheets from 
first to last. His experience with the Winchester Rolls 
has been of the greatest service in this matter, and the 
result of it in his work on ‘‘ The Obedientiary Rolls of 
St. Swithun’s ” will often be found in the use made of that 
volume in my Introduction and Glossary. 

My old friend William Greenwell, the veteran 
archeologist of the North, has always been, like another 
William famed in Border minstrelsy, “‘ good at need.” 
All who have occasion to consult the Chapter MSS. are 
immensely indebted to him for the admirable order in 
which they have been arranged under his direction, and 


INTRODUCTION. Ixvil 


for his readiness to be of use in connexion with them when 
help is required. And, as is mentioned in the Preface to 
Vol. I, it was he who made the suggestion that.led to my 
undertaking this present work. 

Mr. St. John Hope has kindly allowed me to make 
use of the proofs of the book of Canterbury Inventories 
which he is editing in conjunction with Dr. Wickham 
Legg, and also of his MS. extracts from the Norwich 
Sacrists’ Rolls, both which sources of evidence have 
afforded some excellent illustrations. 

Mr. Edward Peacock, F.S.A., of Bottesford Manor, 
has given me access to his collections, and has greatly 
helped me with the Glossary, the whole of which has 
passed under his eye, and has had the benefit of his 
learned judgment. 

The Glossary has also greatly profited by the botanical 
knowledge of my brother, the Rev. William Fowler, M.A., 
Vicar of Liversedge, who has usually been able to send me 
whatever information and references I have wanted in 
connexion with the plants and vegetable products 
mentioned in the Rolls. 

And lastly I wish gratefully to acknowledge the kind- 
ness and the industry of my niece, Miss E. E. Fowler, 
and of other relations and friends who have helped her in 
the long and tedious business of sorting the slips used in 
the formation of the Index. Any one who has made an 
Index extending over 122 octavo pages of two columns 
each will have some idea of what this means. 
| It will readily be believed that this work has cost 
much more labour in the preparation than any of those 
which I have edited hitherto, but I do not consider that 
the labour has been ill bestowed. For it has rendered 
accessible to students a vast amount of material concerning 
the daily life of a great monastic establishment, material, 
moreover, of exceptional interest and variety.

SINCE the issue of the last Report, the Society has to 
deplore the loss of its President, Dr. Stubbs, Bishop of 
Oxford. The world at large is acquainted with his 
eminent merits as an historian, the width and sanity of 
his views being very conspicuous, but to Yorkshire men 
his memory will ever be especially dear from the deep 
interest he took in all antiquarian matters relating to his 
native county, an interest which included even its Parish 
Registers. It must ever be a matter of deep regret that, 
owing to pressure of unavoidable professional engagements, 
he was never able to undertake any work relating 
exclusively to the North of England. At the Annual 
Meeting of the Society, held at Durham on Tuesday, 
June 4th, 1901, the Duke of Northumberland, Ke Gywas 
elected Patron and President, in succession to the Bishop 
of Oxford. His Grace’s high rank and deep and 
intelligent interest in archeological matters point him out 
as pre-eminently suited for this post. The Society has lost 
five of its Vice-Presidents since 1899, the Bishop of 
London, Canon Atkinson, Chancellor R. S. Ferguson 
and Mr. John Sykes, by death, and the Rev. Thomas 
Randell by withdrawal. To Canon Atkinson the Society 
is indebted for editions of the Chartularies of Whitby 
and Rievaulx. The vacant places have been filled 
up by the election of Lord Barnard, Mr. oe We Clay 
Mr. R. O. Heslop, Mr. W. W. Morrell, and Mr. S. J. 
Chadwick. Since the date of the last Report, the 
following volumes have been issued to the members 
of the Society :—Newcastle Adventurers, II]; and York 
Freemen, II. The Council regrets that, from causes 
incidental to the nature of a Society such as this, there are 


4 


considerable arrears in the publication of the volumes. 
As no fewer than six volumes are in the press, it is hoped 
that by the close of the year the publications will be up to 
date. Amongst volumes which may be expected shortly 
are:—The Beverley Chapter Act Book, II, edited by 
Mr. A. F. Leach ; Durham Account Rolls, III, containing 
Index and Glossary, edited by.Canon Fowler ; Testamenta 
Eboracensia, VI, edited by Mr. J. W. Clay, continuing the 
magnificent series of wills from York printed under 
the supervision of the late Canon Raine; a volume of 
Knaresborough Wills, in which the late Bishop of Oxford 
was much interested, edited by Dr. Collins ; a volume 
from the records of the Company of Hoastmen of 
Newcastle, illustrating the history of the coal-trade, edited ~ 
by Mr. F. W. Dendy; and the Register of Walter 
Giffard, Archbishop of York, 1266-1279, edited by the 
Secretary. To enable the Society to continue on its 
successful career and print some of the numerous 
manuscripts worthy of publication, skilled editors, 
possessing local or technical knowledge, and new members, 


are continually wanted to supply the vacancies caused by 
death. 


ir EieSURT EES: SOGIELY, 
ESTABLISHED IN THE YEAR 1834, 


In honour of the late Robert Surtees, of Mainsforth, Esquire, 
the author of the History of the County Palatine of Durham, 
and in accordance with his pursuits and plans; having for its 
object the publication of inedited Manuscripts, illustrative of 
the intellectual, the moral, the religious, and the social 
_ condition of those parts of England and Séotland included on 
the east between the Humber and the Firth of Forth, and on 
the west between the Mersey and the Clyde, a region which 
constituted the ancient Kingdom of Northumbria. 


NEW RULES AGREED UPON IN 1849; REVISED 1863. 


I.—The Society shall consist of not more than three hundred 
and fifty members. 


II1.—There shall be a Patron of the Society, who shall be 
President. 


Il1].—There shall be twenty-four Vice-Presidents, a Secretary, 
and two Treasurers. 


I1V.—The Patron, the Vice-Presidents, the Secretary, and the 
Treasurers, shall form the Council, any five of whom, including 
the Secretary and a Treasurer, shall be a quorum competent to 
transact the business of the Society. 


V.—The twenty-four Vice-Presidents, the Secretary, and the 
Treasurers, shall be elected at a general meeting, to continue in 
office for three years, and be capable of re-election. 


VI.—Any vacancies in the office of Secretary or Treasurers 
shall be provisionally filled up by the Council, subject to the 
approbation of the next general meeting. 


VII.—Three meetings of the Council shall be held in every 
year, on the first Tuesday in the months of. March, June, and 
December ; and the place and hour of meeting shall be fixed by 
the Council, and communicated by the Secretary to the members 
of the Council. 


VIII.—The meeting in June shall be the Anniversary, to 
which all the members of the Society shall be convened by the 
Secretary. 


IX.—The Secretary shall convene extraordinary meetings 
of the Council, on a requisition to that effect, signed by not less 
than five members of the Council, being presented to him. 


6 


X.—-Members may be elected by ballot at any of the ordinary 
meetings, according to priority of application, upon being 
proposed in writing by three existing members. One black ball 
in ten shall exclude. 


XI.—Each member shall pay in advance to the Treasurer the 
annual sum of one guinea. If any member’s subscription shall 
be in arrear for two years, and he shall neglect to pay his 
subscription after having been reminded by the Treasurer, he 
shall be regarded as having ceased to be a member of the 
Society. 

XII,—The money raised by the Society shall be expended in 
publishing such compositions, in their original language, or ina 
translated form, as come within the scope of this Society, 
without limitation of time with reference to the period of their 
respective authors. All editorial and other expenses to be 
defrayed by the Society. 


XIII.—One volume, at least, in a closely printed octavo form, 
shall be supplied to each member of the Society every year, free 
of expense. 


XIV.—If the funds of the Society in any year will permit, the 
Council shall be at liberty to print and furnish to the members, 
free of expense, any other volume or volumes of the same 
character, in the same or a different form. 


XV.—The number of copies of each publication, and the 
selection of a printer and publisher, shall be left to the Council, 
who shall also fix the price at which the copies, not furnished to 
members, shall be sold to the public. 


XVI.—The armorial bearings of Mr. Surtees, and some 
other characteristic decoration connecting the Society with his 
name, shall be used in each publication. 


XVII.—A list of the officers and members, together with an 
account of the receipts and expenses of the Society, shall be 
made up every year to the time of the annual meeting, and shall 
be submitted to the Society to be printed and published with 
the next succeeding volume. 


XVIII.—No alteration shall be made in these rules, except at 
an annual meeting. Notice of any such alteration shall be 
given, at least as early as the ordinary meeting of the Council 
immediately preceding, to be communicated to each member of 
the Society.
